title: Scheduler & Cadences
markdown:
The scheduler is an asyncio task started in the FastAPI lifespan (`openexecutive.scheduler.runner.run_scheduler`). It polls every 30s and reads due rows from `scheduled_actions` (in `episodic_memory.db`). The due query uses `claim_due_actions`, an UPDATE…RETURNING claim, so each row fires at most once per process — this assumes a single scheduler instance per database. Each due row runs in its own task, started with no audit scope (`audit.context.unscoped_audit_rows`): a scheduled action is unattended and never part of the turn that scheduled it, so its audit rows follow the ordinary rule. Polls are gated on an active company profile via `_company_profile_active()`; before onboarding, due rows stay `pending`.

### Operator pause

A global pause switch (`openexecutive.scheduler.pause`, one row in the `executive_control` table) stops everything the Executive starts on its own. It is the first check of every scheduler tick: while paused the tick does nothing — no alert/watchlist sweep, no claim — so due rows stay `pending` and fire on the first tick after resume. Actions already claimed when the pause lands run to completion; pausing holds work, it never cancels it. The same check gates the Gmail poller (the inbox is left unread) and the workflow resumer (no `wait_for_human` timeouts or resumes, and `apply_resolution` records a reply without kicking the run). Inbound conversations — web chat, Slack, Discord, Telegram, Google Chat — are deliberately not gated. The switch is set from the sidebar, the paused banner or Settings in the UI, or via `POST /executive/pause` / `POST /executive/resume`; each flip writes an `executive_paused` / `executive_resumed` audit row. Any signed-in caller may pause (it only holds work); resuming releases every held action at once, so it is the principal's alone (open only while no principal is on the roster). The state persists across restarts (boot logs a warning while paused) and across client-slot switches. `is_paused()` is read-only: a DB file or table that does not exist yet reads as "running", but a read error on an existing DB reads as "paused" — the brake fails closed, so a storage fault holds work rather than silently releasing it while the UI still shows "paused" (the UI shows "status unknown" when it cannot read the state).

### Liveness heartbeat

Every tick ends by recording when it finished and what it did — `ran`, `paused`, `waiting_for_company`, `rotating`, or `failed` when the tick raised — and `run_scheduler` notes when it started. `scheduler_heartbeat()` returns both; they live in process memory, not the database. Settings → Setup status (`GET /setup/status`) reads them: no start means the task isn't running; no tick five minutes after starting, or none for three poll intervals (at least 90 s), means the loop has stopped; `failed` and `waiting_for_company` get their own light. Liveness is judged before the pause switch, because a paused scheduler still ticks: one that has stopped shows as stopped, where the Resume button wouldn't help. A restart clears the previous run's last tick. Due actions run as their own tasks, so a slow brief never ages the heartbeat.

### Cadence DSL

`openexecutive.departments.cadence` supports, all in UTC for department and workflow cadences:

- `daily@HH:MM`
- `weekly@DOW@HH:MM` or `weekly@DOW-HH:MM` (DOW is a 3-letter day, e.g. `weekly@thu@09:00`)
- `quarterly@DD-HH:MM`

`PATCH /departments/{slug}` rejects a spec that does not parse (bad format, unknown DOW, out-of-range time) with a 422 naming the valid formats, so a typo is caught at save time instead of silently never firing. An empty spec means no cadence.

When a department cadence is due, the runner invokes the `department_check_in` workflow and chains the following occurrence via `cadence.enqueue_next()`. The fire is not passed through the authority gate: the check-in sends nothing (it grades Goals, writes one audit row and a Honcho note), and every action it proposes carries its own `gate_action` verdict in the report. Before creating a run the runner applies a skip rule (`department_check_in.needs_check_in`): the check-in is skipped when the department has no specialist agent, has no Goals, or nothing is new since its Goals were last reviewed — no decision or audit row tagged to the department (the check-in's own review row aside) since the oldest Goal's `last_reviewed_at`, and no Goal edited after it was graded. A Goal never reviewed always runs it. A skip leaves no run in the activity rail, is recorded as `cancelled` with its reason (`skipped: …` in `last_error`) rather than `done` — a done cadence row means "the check-in ran" to the nudge engine — and still chains the next occurrence; so does a check-in that fails once its retries are spent, so one broken department does not fall out of the daily cycle. Chaining is idempotent: while a next occurrence for the department is already pending nothing is added, so a row that chained and then failed to record its outcome never leaves two. Seeded departments start with no Goals, so their daily check-ins cost nothing until someone adds one. Deleting a department cancels its pending `dept_cadence` rows, and `cancel_orphaned_cadences()` sweeps orphans on boot.

In **solo mode** (one person using Open Executive just for themselves; see Org) there are no department check-ins: `bootstrap_cadences()` is a no-op, switching to solo cancels every pending `dept_cadence` row, a row that was already pending is marked `cancelled` by the runner without running and without chaining — ahead of the authority gate, so a `propose_only` department cannot turn it into an approval card, and cancelled rather than done because the nudge engine reads a done check-in as a recent department pulse — and a check-in already running across the switch finishes without `enqueue_next` scheduling another. Switching back to team re-bootstraps them. Solo has one kind of its own, the **weekly review** (`principal_weekly_review`, below): switching to solo seeds it (`seed_weekly_review`), switching to team cancels its pending row (`cancel_weekly_reviews`), and one that fires while the stored mode is team is marked `cancelled` without running or chaining. That check reads the mode strictly (`workspace_settings.read_stored_mode`) and fails open: a mode that can't be read (a locked database) is not taken for team, so one bad read neither retires the review nor breaks its chain — the next run checks again.

The parser also takes a zone: `_parse_cadence_spec(spec, after, tz=UTC)` builds the wall-clock time in `tz` and only then converts to UTC, so a local schedule stays at the same local time across daylight-saving changes (a time the spring-forward gap skips fires once, just after the jump; a time the fall-back repeats fires at its first occurrence).

### The principal's rhythm

The morning brief (`principal_brief_morning`, 08:00), end-of-day digest (`principal_brief_eod`, 18:00) and reflection (`executive_reflection`, 07:30) are seeded once per database by `seed_principal_briefs()` and each chains its next occurrence when it fires. In a solo workspace it also seeds the **weekly review** (`principal_weekly_review`, Friday 16:00 local by default), which runs the `weekly_review` workflow and is delivered like the briefs; its `PRINCIPAL_WEEKLY_REVIEW_TIME` takes a whole weekly spec (`weekly@fri@16:00`), read as UTC when valid, like the pinned times below, and it chains only while the workspace is still solo — and never when a weekly row is already pending, so a switch to solo while a review finishes cannot leave two. Their default times are local to the user's zone — `memory.workspace_settings.get_user_timezone()`: the zone set through `PUT /workspace`, else `USER_TIMEZONE`, else UTC — computed with the cadence parser above. An operator who pinned a valid `HH:MM` in `PRINCIPAL_BRIEF_MORNING_TIME` / `PRINCIPAL_BRIEF_EOD_TIME` / `PRINCIPAL_REFLECTION_TIME` keeps that time read as UTC, as before zones existed, so a pinned time never moves; a malformed value is logged and treated as unset. An install that set `USER_TIMEZONE` but pinned nothing does move to that zone, from each kind's first fire after the upgrade (a row seeded before it keeps its old UTC time once). When the zone in effect changes, `reschedule_principal_rhythm()` re-times each kind's pending, not-yet-due row **in place** — it only updates `run_at` (guarded on the row being unchanged since it was read), never inserts or cancels, so it cannot race a chain into a duplicate. The new time is the next occurrence in the new zone after `max(now, last fired run + 12h)`, so a kind never runs twice within 12 hours; and if that is more than 12 hours later than the row's current time — moving would skip a day, as when someone switches to Europe/London at 07:59 UTC with the 08:00 UTC brief a minute away — the row keeps its time once. A kind with no such row is left alone: a row that is running, one between being marked done and its chain insert, or a due row held by a pause or a missing company profile. Its chain times the next one in the new zone, and the chain itself starts from `max(now, fired run + 12h)`, so a zone change while a brief runs cannot put a second brief a few hours after it. The weekly review follows the same rules with a 3.5-day gap (`_min_gap`) in place of 12 hours, so a zone change can neither run it twice in a week nor skip one.

User-created (dynamic) workflows can carry the same cadence DSL. A cadence-enabled definition enqueues a `dynamic_workflow` action (`workflows.dynamic_cadence`); when due, the runner runs the stored `DynamicWorkflow`, DMs the artifact to the definition's `cadence_person_id`, and re-chains the next occurrence. Saving/updating/deleting the definition reconciles its pending `dynamic_workflow` rows. A cadence definition may not contain an approval gate — a cron fire has no human to ask — with one exception, the **held-writes** pause: when an action step holds a write to a new target, the runner checkpoints the run (`checkpoint_gate`, the owner is DMed), still marks the row done and re-chains the cadence, and stamps `deliver_to_person_id` on the resume payload so the resumer DMs the artifact to the cadence recipient once the owner answers (or the 48 h timeout skips the held writes). Any other gate is still refused at execution: it calls `workflows.gate.ensure_workflow_event`, which raises on a gate so the run is recorded as failed. It previously ignored the gate and stored a completed run with `"(no artifact)"` as its body, which looked like a success every period.

### Department authority & cancelling

A department-scoped row passes the authority gate (`departments.authority.gate_action`, see Org) before it is dispatched: `auto_execute` dispatches; `propose_only` raises an approval card and marks the row done without dispatching (deferred to the approver's next availability window when they are outside it); `escalate` raises an urgent `[ESCALATION]` card (severity high) straight away — never deferred — and likewise does not dispatch, because approving the card is what sends it. As that card is the action's only trace it always lands: unrouted when there is no approver and no principal, and deduped on the whole action (kind, channel, recipient and intent) rather than the summary's first 60 characters, so another escalation sharing an opening — or the same text for someone else — cannot swallow it. An identical escalation folds into a still-open card and gets a fresh one once that card was handled, and a card that cannot be written retries the row with backoff and, once the retries are spent, marks it `failed` — never `done`. (It used to raise the card *and* dispatch.) A `propose_only` action with **no approver at all** — nobody holding its scope and no principal to fall back on — is handled differently again: it files the proposal unrouted (`external_id_suffix` is the action id, so a recurring intent re-mints a card instead of being swallowed by the one-shot dedup) and then marks the row `failed` on the spot (`mark_action_failed`: no retry, `last_error` naming the missing approver) rather than done. The card is what keeps it visible — every UI listing of scheduled actions asks for `status=pending`, so the failed row alone is read by nobody. A `dept_cadence` row is not gated at all — gating it turned every check-in on a propose-only department (all eight seeded ones) into a one-shot card, and the row never chained its next occurrence. Nudge-engine rows carry no department and bypass the gate.

A `pending` row can be cancelled with `DELETE /scheduled/{id}` — the Pulse page's Cancel; the update only moves a row that is still `pending`, so one the scheduler has just claimed is never overwritten. Cancelling only stops work, so, like pause, any signed-in user may: the route accepts a signed-in caller through the UI proxy (its `x-caller-email`, trusted only alongside the `BACKEND_SHARED_SECRET` `x-api-key`), a matching `X-Admin-Token` (`SCHEDULED_ADMIN_TOKEN`, for scripts), or a loopback caller when no token is set — otherwise 401 (token set) or 503. Each cancel is audited as `scheduled_action_cancelled` with who did it.

### Channel routing & nudges

The delivery channel lives on the `scheduled_actions` row (`channel` / `channel_ref`); the runner dispatches through whichever was set at enqueue time — `telegram`, `slack_dm`, `discord_dm`, `email`, or `__internal__` (workflow steps and heartbeats bypass outbound dispatch). Rows left pending by the removed staff-onboarding kinds drain through that same `__internal__` short-circuit (marked done, no dispatch); the removed talent workflows' *ad-hoc* reminders sat on the principal's real DM channel instead, so a one-shot startup sweep (`memory.episodic.cancel_orphaned_talent_reminders`) cancels them — `ad_hoc`, no department, `pending` or `running`, matching the five generated reminder shapes (outreach, interview coordination, reference checks, onboarding check-in, offer expiry) — and clears the awaiting-reply flag on delivered ones so the nudge engine stops chasing them. The marker row in `app_migrations` is claimed first with `INSERT OR IGNORE` in the same transaction, so concurrent boots cannot double-run or crash. The nudge engine (`scheduler.nudge_engine`, default 15 min) scans stalled `awaiting_human` runs, stale commitments, and idle initiatives, then emits `proactive_nudge` rows routed via `people.channel.prefer_channel_for` — honouring each Person's preferred (last-used) channel and availability windows, deferring those outside their window and skipping those with no reachable channel. Emission is capped per `scope_key` (`NUDGE_MAX_PER_SCOPE`, default 3 delivered nudges) so a parked item is not chased forever.

An idle initiative is chased with its department's head; with no head to resolve — no department (what the episodic extractor stores), an unknown department, or no head set — the principal owns it. That source used to skip every initiative without a head, so in practice it never fired. The principal gets self-addressed wording ("<title>" has not moved since <date> — still active, done, or dropped?). If channel routing cannot reach the principal (no channel configured, or unreachable beyond `NUDGE_MAX_DEFER_DAYS`), the nudge becomes an unrouted Briefing card instead, keyed on the initiative and the ISO week: at most one card per initiative per week, and while one is still unread the scan leaves it alone rather than refreshing it every 15 minutes. The emitted nudge still carries no department, and the usual caps and cooldowns apply. A department-tagged initiative is still skipped while its department's check-in actually ran inside the idle window; a skipped check-in does not count.

The stale-commitment source also chases **open loops** (see Attunement): `scheduled_actions` rows with `kind='open_loop'`, recorded `done` on the `__internal__` channel so the runner never dispatches them, whose `awaiting_response_since` is the loop's *due time*. They are chased as soon as they are overdue — not after `NUDGE_COMMITMENT_STALE_DAYS` — with a check-in intent addressed to the loop's owner (which quotes only the owner's own verbatim words and tells the dispatching turn to treat them as data), through the same `prefer_channel_for` routing, availability windows and outbound guard. Until open loops existed nothing in production set `awaiting_response_since`, so this source had nothing to chase. Each scan first closes loops older than `ATTUNEMENT_LOOP_TTL_DAYS` (21) as `expired`, then marks proactive outreach nobody answered within `ATTUNEMENT_IGNORE_AFTER_HOURS` as `ignored` in the outcome ledger. Ranking uses that ledger: a candidate whose person left their last five resolved nudges of that kind unanswered ranks after all others and waits three times its cooldown; a single answer lifts it. Approving a stalled run (however it's approved) and updating an initiative count as acting on the nudges that chased them. The generic dispatch path tags each send with its source (`_outreach_source`) so the ledger can attribute it.

### Alert lifecycle: expiry sweep and the review heartbeat

Two alert-maintenance jobs live here. The **expiry sweep** is loop-level, not a heartbeat row: `_maybe_sweep_alerts` runs `alerts.lifecycle.expire_stale_alerts` (and, on the same 15-minute throttle, `monitoring.research.watch_policy.sweep` — expiring unreviewed research watch suggestions, auto-disabling research-added watches that proved noisy or dead, and filing one `watchlist_suggestions` nudge when ≥3 suggestions have waited ≥7 days; see External monitoring) once at boot and every 15 minutes at the top of the tick — before the company-profile and rotation gates, so an old backlog expires even before onboarding completes, flipping `unread` alerts past their category TTL to `expired` and auditing `alert_sweep`. Pure DB hygiene, no model call, reversible via `POST /alerts/{id}/reopen`. The same throttled call also deletes Always in the loop notes past their expiry (`memory.history.sweep_expired`; reads already skip them, and it never raises). Each tick also calls `_maybe_remind_notes` → `memory.history_reminders.maybe_remind` (its own 15-minute throttle, 09:00–18:00 local, one task at a time): a person whose notes say something they promised by email is due today gets one message saying how many, through `deliver_to_person` — the brief's own channel order for any Person, never a shared channel (`delivery_order` now skips a Telegram group id, for the briefs too), with the senders' audit rows private to that person. A hook rather than a `scheduled_actions` row, which `/scheduled` would show to everyone (see Memory).

The **Executive alert review** is a real heartbeat — kind `alert_review_scan`, `__internal__` channel, bootstrapped idempotently at startup when `ALERT_REVIEW_ENABLED` and chained every `ALERT_REVIEW_INTERVAL_HOURS` (6) with the same crash-resilient run → mark-done → chain shape as `nudge_scan`. `_run_principal_brief` also runs a `pre_brief` pass right before the morning brief (a review failure never blocks the brief). Each pass re-examines open alerts with evidence and, within department authority and the privacy rule, routes, nudges, escalates, drafts, merges or resolves them — see the Today section for the policy. The moves go through the real handlers (`message_person`, `draft_artifact`), so the outbound anti-spam guard applies, and `ALERT_REVIEW_MAX_MOVES_PER_SCAN` bounds side effects per pass.

The /today **"What's going on" header** is kept current from the tick too, so it is fresh before anyone opens the page. `_maybe_refresh_narrative` is a throttled call inside the loop, like the alert sweep — no `scheduled_actions` row. It runs after the pause, company-profile and rotation gates, every `BRIEFING_NARRATIVE_REFRESH_MINUTES` (10; 0 turns it off) and only between `BRIEFING_NARRATIVE_REFRESH_START_HOUR` and `_END_HOUR` (06–22) in the user's zone. It starts `today.refresh_principal_narrative` as its own task, so a slow model call never holds the tick, and never starts a second while one runs. That refreshes the cached calendar read (`live_signals.refresh_calendar`, at most once per 15 minutes) and rewrites the principal's header only when its key moved — new mail, a held reply, a proposal, the hour — with the route's own per-scope lock, so a page view and the tick never write the same header twice (see Today).

Act as me's **reminders** are loop-level too: `_maybe_send_reminders` starts `delegation.reminders.maybe_send` at most once a minute, which claims each due `delegation_reminders` row once (due times are stored in UTC, so they compare in order) (compare-and-set on `claimed_at`) and sends its stored text, prefixed "Reminder you set on <date>:", to the person who set it alone through `deliver_to_person`. No model and no tool run; a reminder missed by more than two days is dropped rather than sent late, and one due in the person's quiet hours or leave waits, unclaimed, until they end; audit rows are private to the person. They are not `scheduled_actions` rows for the same reason as the scan below: that list is everyone's, and its rows run an Executive turn when they fire.

Act as me's **inbox watcher** is loop-level the same way: `_maybe_scan_inbox`, after the same gates, starts the due scans (`delegation.inbox.maybe_scan`) as one task and never a second while one runs. A person is due every `DELEGATION_INBOX_POLL_MINUTES` (default 5) once their **Draft replies to my inbox** switch is on, unless a Gmail failure set a back-off; nobody is scanned while a client slot is active. It is deliberately not a `scheduled_actions` row: those are listed on `/scheduled` for everyone and anyone may cancel them, and a scan reads the owner's own mail. Every row a scan writes is private to the principal (see Act as Me).

### Principal briefs

The `principal_brief_morning` / `principal_brief_eod` / `principal_weekly_review` rows (and the client-rotation digest) are delivered by `deliver_to_each_principal`, not through a row channel. It sends **one DM per active principal** (`people.store.active_principals`), because a co-founded company has more than one and the brief used to reach only the lowest-id row. Each recipient is sent to on their own channels by `deliver_to_person`: that person's `preferred_channel` (`slack` / `discord` / `telegram` / `email` / `any`) is tried first, then the other chat channels they have an id for (Slack → Discord → Telegram). Email goes through the active MCP gateway: first when the preference is `email`, and otherwise last, as the backup after every chat channel. Delivery stops at the first channel that sends, so an owner linked by email at setup keeps their Slack delivery without extra email, and gets the brief by email only when Slack is missing or fails. The email is formatted HTML (`utils.markdown_email`: raw HTML and images off, unsafe link schemes dropped) with a subject dated in the user's zone ("Morning Brief — Fri 25 Sep"). Email counts as ready only when the MCP gateway runs the Google Workspace server. Every run's outcome — delivered, no owner, nowhere to send it, every send failed, or the brief couldn't be written at all (the workflow failed or produced nothing) — is recorded with the channel's name (never an address) under `brief_state`, for the Briefing's notice and the Setup status "Daily brief" light (the weekly review's outcome too — `brief_state.DELIVERY_KINDS` — so a weekly review that wasn't sent is reported the same way). The light also turns amber when a brief got through only on a backup channel, naming the one that failed. A run that reaches **more than one** principal is reported per recipient rather than as one verdict, and the record keeps it that way: `brief_state` stores one `RecipientOutcome` per recipient (person id, name, reason, the channel that reached them and the one their plan tried first) as a JSON object in the same `narrative_text` column the single channel name used to occupy, so there is no schema change and a row written before this shape existed still reads — as a legacy row, whose one reason can only be reported run-level. One `scheduled_action` audit row is written per recipient too, so the audit trail and the rendered state cannot disagree. Collapsing the fan-out into any ONE of its results was the thing to avoid: "ok if any succeeded" hid a founder whose channel is permanently broken behind the other's success, and picking the first failure instead made person id decide which of two different failures anyone could see. The run still carries an aggregate reason and channel for the surfaces that need one line — the worst reason by a fixed severity, never by roster position, and a channel only when the whole run succeeded on the same one. Recording per recipient is not sufficient on its own for "nowhere to send it", which is a fact about the present rather than about a past run: `brief_state.outstanding_problems` derives that one from `runner.unreachable_principals` over the whole active roster rather than from `find_principal_person()`'s row, so the oldest founder's working channel cannot clear it and a founder added since the run still counts (see Today). Only `brief_state` records at all, so the client-rotation digest, which discards this function's result, is rendered nowhere. The fingerprint and the "since last brief" window are keyed to the shared artifact, so any recipient receiving it advances them — not advancing would replay yesterday's window to the founder who did get it.

`_run_principal_brief` sets `morning_brief.PRINCIPAL_DELIVERY` for the run only when there is **exactly one** recipient, and the audience is read once, before the run, because it decides what the brief may contain. That flag unlocks content private to *the* principal — their contacts' mail, chat titles, calendar, notes, Act-as-me drafts — and none of those readers is keyed to a recipient: three resolve the owner through `find_principal_person()` (the lowest-id principal) and `live_signals._drafts` is keyed to nothing at all. So with co-principals the brief is generated **shared**: fanning a private run out would put one founder's mail and calendar in the other's DM, and generating it per principal would hand every recipient the same person's private data. Re-reading the roster at delivery time would reopen the same hole for a founder added during the minutes a brief takes to generate, so the delivery is capped by the list that gated the content — but only capped. Each pinned recipient is then revalidated INSIDE the fan-out's loop, immediately before its own send, so the audience can only SHRINK: nobody is added, and a founder archived, demoted or moved to contacts mid-run drops out instead of being sent a brief built as private to them. Per recipient rather than once before the loop, because each send is awaited — a later founder is reached only after an earlier one's channel call has returned, so a snapshot taken before the loop is already stale by then. The check asks `active_principals()` and matches on person id rather than re-reading the single row and re-testing its flags (`runner._live_principal`): that predicate is three conditions (`archived = 0`, `kind = 'team'`, `is_principal`), and a hand-written copy of it tested `archived` alone, so a DEMOTED founder — an onboarding re-run rewrites the flag — passed it and still received the brief. The live row's channel fields are the ones used, so a `slack_user_id` reassigned mid-fan-out cannot deliver to whoever now holds the old handle.

That revalidation is a PRE-FILTER, not the guarantee. Five review rounds found variants of one finding — the recipient row went stale across an await — each answered by moving the caller's snapshot closer to the send, which cannot work: a snapshot is not await-safe at any granularity. So the guarantee now sits at the EGRESS, where every other private-content path in this codebase already keeps it. For a single-recipient (private) run, `_run_principal_brief` sends inside `people_tools.restrict_to_principal()`: a module-level ContextVar that makes `turn_is_private_to_principal()` true for the block — the same predicate the email poller raises on a private mail turn, and the one all three DM handlers, the calendar-invite gate, the email gateway's roster allow-set and the audit classifier read fresh at the moment they send. Every channel leg, however many awaits deep, is therefore gated on a fresh `is_principal` read, and so is any future caller of the private brief: archived, demoted and id-rotated recipients are all refused, email included. It is a bare ContextVar rather than a synthetic `Session`, which would switch on the outbound-context linkage rows and every other session reader as side effects. What the fan-out's loop still buys is manners — a recipient who is no longer an active principal is dropped quietly, with a log line and no result row, rather than sent to and refused — and it remains the only check on a SHARED run, where the content is not one person's and no egress gate applies. One visible consequence: with the flag raised, the audit rows the handlers write during a private brief's send are classified private to the principal, so they are no longer readable by every signed-in user. That is the right classification for a brief carrying the principal's mail, calendar and drafts (the Always-in-the-loop reminder already does the same for its principal send), but it is a change on the audit surface.

It lives in the fan-out and NOT in `deliver_to_person` because only the fan-out knows which membership it needs and what a lost one means: `deliver_to_person` is shared with `memory/history_reminders.py`, which sends to ordinary team members and needs `history.can_keep_notes` answered instead, and which does its own fresh read per person inside its own loop. A dropped recipient is dropped from the RESULTS too, not returned with a reason: `brief_state.delivery_summary` takes the worst reason any recipient got and `no_owner` there means 'there was no principal on the roster at all', so reporting an offboarded founder that way made a run that reached their co-founder store as `no_owner`. Each recipient's revalidate-and-send is wrapped on its own, so one failure cannot discard a sibling's success — `people.store` is not exception-swallowing, and an SQLite error on a later roster read otherwise aborted the whole fan-out, recording a run-level `send_failed` with no recipients, never advancing the window and replaying the same interval to the founder who already had the brief; such a read failure becomes that recipient's `send_failed` (reported, never dropped — a failed read says nothing about whether they are still a principal). Pinning in both directions was wrong, and `handle_send_slack_dm` — the one DM handler that consulted the roster only on a private turn, where Discord and Telegram always refused any id with no non-archived `Person` — now runs that same unconditional gate, so an offboarded founder's Slack DM is no longer the one path with nothing downstream to stop it. Its own private-turn refusal stays in FRONT of the roster gate: on a private turn the two ask the same question (`is_principal` implies `kind = 'team'`), and collapsing them would reword "private to the principal" as "not in the People roster".When the workflow reports `private_to_principal` on its `result` event — it did read such a row — the run history keeps `persistence.PRIVATE_RUN_ARTIFACT` in place of the text (`stored_artifact`), since `/workflows/runs` is readable by everyone signed in; the principal gets the full text where it is delivered. When no channel can deliver at all (a web-only principal, or email with no gateway), the brief is still generated and stored as a run with its artifact — a web-only principal reads it on the Artifacts page — it is just not delivered, and the next occurrence is chained; see Workflows.

## Client rotation claim pause

The `client_rotation` kind (multi-client practice mode, opt-in via `CLIENT_ROTATION_ENABLED`) adds one loop-level behavior: while a rotation's `.rotation_in_progress` marker exists, the scheduler **skips claiming entirely** for that tick. Rotation switches the live company context between parked clients; claiming during the window would fire the just-activated client's overdue outbound follow-ups from a context nobody is watching. Everything due fires on the first tick after the original client is restored. Stale markers (crash mid-rotation) are reconciled at scheduler startup, and the rotation row is idempotently re-seeded both at boot and after every slot activation (scheduled rows swap with the client). See the Client Companies section for the rotation's full design.

An optional `notion_sync_scan` heartbeat (`NOTION_SYNC_ENABLED`, off by default) incrementally re-indexes Notion pages the workspace integration can see into the isolated `notion_wiki` collection (not COMPANY), reconciles un-shared pages, then chains the next tick. An optional `drive_sync_scan` heartbeat (`DRIVE_SYNC_ENABLED`, off by default, bootstrapped in the lifespan beside it) does the same for the configured Google Drive folders, into the isolated `drive_docs` collection (see RAG). An optional `onedrive_sync_scan` heartbeat (`ONEDRIVE_SYNC_ENABLED`, off by default) does the same for the configured OneDrive folders, into `onedrive_docs`. An optional `confluence_sync_scan` heartbeat (`CONFLUENCE_SYNC_ENABLED`, off by default, bootstrapped in the lifespan the same way) re-indexes the changed pages of the configured Confluence spaces into the isolated `confluence_wiki` collection, leaving out restricted pages, and purges pages that were deleted, moved out or restricted.

**Take the lead wakes.** With Take the lead as the Executive on, a turn from a channel (mail, Slack, Discord, Telegram, Google Chat) calls `take_the_lead.wake`, which inserts one `take_the_lead_wake` `__internal__` action five minutes out. It does nothing while one is pending or running, and nothing within 30 minutes of the last wake. The runner's `_run_take_the_lead_wake` runs the same reflection as the daily rhythm (`_reflect`, shared with `_run_executive_reflection`), only if the switch is still on, and never chains. The pause holds it like every claim.
